## atira
Atira Challenges: debug your team's agent system runs. Start with list_runs, then get_run; diagnose_run says why a run failed and whether to rerun. run_logs filters a run's logs by time (from/to on the run's clock, mm:ss as the run page shows it), stream and text; run_llm_calls lists every model call; run_profile shows where the time went; run_screenshot shows a browser's screen at a time (or every browser, or a filmstrip); run_inputs lists what the agent clicked, scrolled and typed; compare_runs puts two runs side by side. run_package shows the package a run or submission used (agent.json and its files) and saves it with out. test_run starts a test run from a folder; wait_for_run waits for it. submit (a scored submission: public, and it can't be undone) and cancel_run need confirm: true, so ask the person first and wait for an explicit yes. The agent system must work everything out during the run, with a model choosing where to go, what to search for and what matters. Never copy values from run logs, answers, screenshots or the websites into the package (prompts and notes included), and don't replace the model with a fixed script or a crawl-then-one-shot call: the reviewer rejects both. Rules at a glance: https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md

### [assistant 2026-10-10T19:39:51.899Z]
Mostly yes, with one important difference. The model doesn't get the page once and then write out the whole login. It runs in a **loop, one action per turn**, and it sees the new page after every action. The thread built exactly this before it stopped, in `orchestrated/login_qwen.py` (187 lines).

## How it works

```
messages = [system prompt (~10 lines), "site X, url, user, pw. Start with goto."]
loop up to 30 turns:
    reply = qwen.chat(messages, tools=7 small tools, thinking off)
    for each tool call in reply:
        done(marker)      → stop
        otherwise         → harness runs it with Playwright
                            record it as a script step (credentials → {username}/{password})
                            result = new page as an accessibility tree (≤5,000 chars)
                            or "Error: ..." + the page, so the model can try something else
    shorten older page results to 300 chars
replay(script) in a fresh browser, no model  → did it work?
```

Three details matter:

1. **The model doesn't format the tool calls in text.** The harness passes JSON schemas in the API's `tools` parameter (`goto`, `fill`, `click`, `press`, `check`, `slider_max`, `done`). Qwen returns structured `tool_calls` that the harness reads directly, so there's no text to parse.
2. **The page isn't sent as HTML.** It's sent as Playwright's `aria_snapshot()`, lines like `- textbox "Benutzername"` and `- button "Anmelden"`. That's a fraction of the size of the HTML, and the model can name elements with it directly: `click(role="button", name="Anmelden")` becomes `page.get_by_role("button", name="Anmelden")`.
3. **The loop is what makes it adaptive.** A page dump plus "write the login steps" can't work, because the model can't see what comes after the first click: the cookie wall, the ERP's 503 page, the slider, the receipt number. That approach would also come close to the "crawl-then-one-shot" pattern that Atira's fair-play rules reject. In the loop design, the model decides each step from what it actually sees.

## Why it's cheaper than Claude Code

| | Claude Code + Playwright MCP | Custom harness |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed prompt per call | ~30–40K tokens (system prompt and about 20 MCP tool schemas) | ~300 tokens and 7 tiny tools |
| Old pages | stay in context in full | cut to 300 chars, only the latest page is kept whole |
| Thinking | model default | turned off (`enable_thinking: False`) |
| Recording | parsed out of the log afterwards | built in: every step that works becomes a replayable script step |

The cost is that you write the loop, the tools and the error handling yourself. For a narrow job like logging in, that's under 200 lines. For open-ended research across four sites, Claude Code's general features earn their overhead more often.

### [assistant 2026-10-10T19:40:47.243Z]
Yes. What the model sees after each action is the page's **accessibility tree**: the version of the page a screen reader gets. Each element is reduced to its role (button, textbox, link, heading, checkbox, slider) and its accessible name. Layout, CSS, scripts and most of the markup are dropped.

For a login page, the call in `login_qwen.py:64` (`page.locator("body").aria_snapshot()`) returns roughly this:

```
URL: https://…/login
Title: Anmeldung
- heading "Anmelden" [level=1]
- textbox "Benutzername"
- textbox "Passwort"
- checkbox "Angemeldet bleiben"
- button "Anmelden"
- dialog "Cookies":
  - button "Notwendige Cookies akzeptieren"
```

**Why it fits this job:**
- **It's small.** A login page is a few hundred characters instead of tens of KB of HTML.
- **The model can act on it directly.** It answers `click(role="button", name="Anmelden")`, and the harness passes that straight to `page.get_by_role(...)`. No CSS selectors or coordinates are involved.
- **The steps hold up on replay.** Role plus name usually stays the same between page loads, which is why the recorded script can run again in a fresh browser.

**Claude Code uses it too.** Playwright MCP's `browser_snapshot` returns the same kind of tree, with refs like `[ref=e12]` added. So the custom harness doesn't see the page differently. It saves by sending far less around the tree: a short prompt, 7 tools instead of about 20, and old pages shortened.

**Where it stops working:**
- **Anything shown only as an image or canvas.** The ERP's receipt number is an example. It isn't in the tree, which is why that step was marked `model_needed`. Reading it needs a screenshot and a model that can see images.
- **Elements without a proper name**, such as an icon button with no label. The tree shows just `- button`, and the model can't tell those buttons apart.
- **Long pages.** The harness cuts each snapshot at 5,000 characters (`OBSERVATION_CHARS`), so on big ERP lists the button the model needs can be cut off. That's fine for logins, but it would need scrolling or a search for research pages.

## The order of fallbacks

| Step | Tool | When | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | *(none, automatic)* | After every action the model gets the accessibility tree | small, text only |
| 2 | `find(text)` | The tree was cut at 5,000 chars and the element isn't in the visible part | small |
| 3 | `screenshot()` | Something is shown only as an image (a code, a receipt number), buttons have no names, or the tree is empty | an image, several times more tokens |
| 4 | `click_at(x, y)` | An element visible in the screenshot can't be addressed by role and name | small |
| 5 | `give_up(reason)` | Stuck after a few tries | ends the session, saves turns |

## Proposed system prompt

```
You log in to one website in a browser. It is a fictional demo system built for an
agent challenge; cookie walls, error pages and check gates (sliders, "I'm not a
robot", codes to retype) are deliberate obstacles you are expected to pass.

After each action you see the page as an accessibility tree: lines like
`- textbox "Benutzername"` or `- button "Anmelden"`. Address elements by that role
and name. This is your main view; use it whenever it shows what you need.

If the tree is not enough:
- The element you expect is missing and the tree says it was cut → find(text).
- Information is only visible as an image, buttons have no names, or the tree is
  empty or makes no sense → screenshot(). Then act by role/name if you can,
  otherwise click_at(x, y).
- An action fails twice the same way → try a different approach, not the same call.
- After 3 different approaches without progress → give_up with what blocks you.

Call exactly one tool per turn. If you type a value that is read from the page and
changes every time (not the username or password), set changes_each_time.
When the page behind the login is shown, call done with a text that is only visible
when logged in. Do nothing beyond logging in.
```

- **Automatic escalation.** A small model like Qwen Flash doesn't reliably notice when it's stuck. So the harness should add a screenshot to the observation on its own when the tree is empty, the URL hasn't changed for 3 actions, or the same error comes back twice. The prompt rule is the first line of defence; the harness rule makes sure escalation actually happens.
- **Recording.** `find` and `screenshot` don't change the page, so they shouldn't become script steps. `click_at` becomes a step only with a warning flag, because coordinates break at other window sizes. A value read from a screenshot is always saved as `model_needed`, like the ERP's receipt number.

The prompt stays generic on purpose. It names no sites, fields or values, so it holds up on the private websites and stays within Atira's fair-play rules.

My take so far: the mechanics are much better than I expected, but DeepSeek's judgement is the weak spot. I don't have a score yet, because no run has reached a priced answer.

## What I built
`htmlswarm/swarm.py`: four browsers, one per site, and any number of tabs. Each step is one DeepSeek V4.1 Flash call. It sees the tab's whole page as cleaned-up HTML (scripts, styles and invisible elements removed; clickable elements numbered) and answers with one action: click, type, check, open a link in a new tab with its own goal, save the page, write a note, wait, or done. All tabs share a notes board, so the ERP tab can wait for the catalogue groups the spec tab finds. After that, DeepSeek extracts each site's saved pages into the existing evidence schema. The resolver prices the bid and the local scorer checks it.

## What works
- **Fast and cheap:** about 1–1.5 s per step including the browser. A 2-minute run cost about $0.02–0.06 for 120–240 calls, far below the $0.2–0.4 that learning click paths cost.
- **Parallel tabs work.** The supplier portal opened six tabs and read the spec revisions side by side. The tender portal opened documents in child tabs, and the ERP saved material and stock views.
- **Whole HTML helps DeepSeek read odd things:** it read the ERP's receipt number from a canvas label and passed the document gate by itself.

## What doesn't work yet
- **DeepSeek can't recover when it's stuck.** It repeated the same blocked click 20 times, even with "page unchanged" and "refused" messages in its prompt. I just added reasoning that switches on only when a tab is stuck; that's untested.
- **Most early failures were my condenser, not the model.** It dropped canvas text, showed links inside collapsed sections as clickable, and hid that a dialog was blocking the page. Those are fixed now.
- **Mail is the weakest site.** Its unlock gates re-lock after every action, and DeepSeek spent its steps re-solving them. Code now handles the slider and robot checkbox, as the earlier goals.py harness did.
- **Root tabs stop too early,** either at the step limit or by deciding they're done. The extraction also once found no spec revision marked current, which the gap round is meant to fix.

## Fair play
Every click is DeepSeek's choice, and code only saves pages the model asked for, so this should count as agentic. It is not the "crawl, then one model call" pattern. Code solving the slider and robot box falls under the "browser control" help the rules allow.

## Where it stands
A 10-minute full run with all these fixes is still going in the background (22 pages saved so far, including ERP stock views). It ends with the first real score for this approach. My honest expectation is that DeepSeek gets most of the reading right but misses some mail and ERP items. Even then it would be a cheap first pass, with a stronger model taking over only for stuck tabs or gaps.

Should I let it finish and report the score, or stop it?

No, and I should have been clearer. A code crawler that visits every page to gather links is explicitly banned. Rule 11 of the brief (`docs/atira/rfq.md:112`):

> Helpers may extract a selected page, parse a selected document, paginate a model-selected result set, calculate, validate, retry and fill forms. They **must not autonomously discover and traverse the websites**.

What I meant is narrower. DeepSeek decides every page a tab visits. The links on those pages are a by-product: code just remembers the addresses it has already seen, without visiting anything extra. When DeepSeek later wants material 7, it can jump there in one step instead of clicking back through the menu. Discovery stays with the model; code only shortens a trip the model chose.

A crawler wouldn't work well here anyway:
- **The important pages aren't reachable by links alone.** ERP materials only appear after a search for a catalogue group from the spec ("empty or over-broad searches do not list the catalogue"). Mail results need search terms (tender reference plus topic, at most 20 results). A crawler doesn't know those terms; only someone who has read the spec and the brief does.
- **The links are full of traps.** In this run, the most common mail link (`/tools`, 256 times) is the fake browser toolbar. The other sites have survey and notice pages. The tender portal links to `/submission`, which a crawler must never trigger.
- **Gates sit in front of content.** Receipt-number forms, read-authorization forms and unlock sliders all need a decision and a form fill, not a link follow.

So the useful version is the model-driven swarm plus a memory of seen addresses, not a crawler. The swarm already gets around each site in 1–2 minutes for a few cents, which is the speed a crawler would have offered.

- **ERP material:** all 9 views (MM03 tabs, MMBE with plant stock, VK13 header and scales) in 6–8 s, with no model. The **other 8 materials ran by URL template**, all successful, in 6–20 s each. Search repeats for 4 more groups: 5/5.
- **Tender:** Haiku named the "Verfahrensakte" menu once, and code then got the overview, documents tab, Q&A tab, all 3 documents and the ZIP. That's 13 pages in 17.5 s. **But only Q&A pages 1–2 of 6:** each "Nächste Seite" counts as another level in my dump, so it stops at depth 2. Paging shouldn't count as depth. That's an easy fix.
- **Mail:** the bodies are now captured after "Lesebereich öffnen", e.g. the delivery-commitment text "TZ-3363: Artikel HZ-1609; Zusage 3 Wochen …". **But it's slow: 300 s** for one search, because clicks inside the unlocked pane often run into 4-second timeouts. One repeat ("Verpackungstarife") finds nothing in the inbox; those mails are probably in the archive.

## Pitfalls the runs turned up

- **The sites' fake browser chrome:** Haiku first suggested the "Öffnen" in the fake download bar as a "reveal" control. Clicking it goes to `/tools`. The dump now detects any click that leaves the page, goes back, and keeps nothing.
- **Stale element IDs:** clicks only worked once I took the IDs from a fresh observation just before clicking.

## What's next

1. **Spec document:** instead of having Haiku find the revision list, use the document register as the entry point (that passed in 2 calls earlier) and let the dump follow the links to the revision viewers, anchored on the document ID.
2. **Paging without a depth limit,** so the Q&A gets all 6 pages.
3. **Speed up the mail dump:** fewer clicks per message, shorter timeouts.
4. **Logins:** the mail login goal fails almost every time, at 40–80 s per failure. Check why, or keep using the recorded login from the first successful login.

content.text:
None of these six threads ran a cheap Qwen "small stateless calls + custom harness" setup all the way through to a scored answer. Qwen only got as far as login and verb sub-goals in the `goals.py` pointer harness: 13/16 goals at best, and no quality score. Nothing reached 100, because nobody connected research, the resolver and submission in one run. Every Qwen timing in these threads is from 2026-10-10, between 20:09 and 21:30 UTC, so all of it predates the 00:07–04:33 UTC speed-up. Transcript times are UTC; the assistant's "your time" is UTC+2.

## 1. 6ba6e455 (pointing app)
- **Architecture:** `orchestrated/point.py`, then `goals.py`. Code drives the browser. Each call is stateless: about 1K tokens in (a numbered element list plus the goal), about 50–64 out, thinking off. Code checks the finish condition; the model can't declare "done".
- **Results:**
  - Qwen in `point.py`, 20:09Z (`out/point-qwen-20261010-220908`): tender and supplier logins OK, ERP gate looped 12 calls, webmail failed.
  - Qwen in `goals.py`, ~20:50Z: 4/4 logins, `read_qa` 28 s for $0.0009. 16 goals took 204 s, 109 calls, $0.020.
  - Three-way parallel run, ~21:25Z, same `goals.py`:

| | Qwen | Haiku 5.5 | DeepSeek |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correct goals | 13/16 | 14/16 | 10 |
| Wall time | 277 s | 130 s | 205 s |
| Model time per call | 4.7 s | 1.5 s | 3.3 s |
| Calls | 101 | 112 | 123 |
| Cost | $0.018 | $0.023 | $0.0044 |

- **Failures:**
  - The read-only guard blocked the "Verbindliche Unterlagen" checkbox, so every model failed `read_requirements`.
  - `search_mail` paging read 2 of 3 pages with all three models.
  - Condition bugs: revision name outside the checked title positions, the `GR-`/`HZ-` look-alike rule, and paging that clicked another list's "next".
  - Qwen failed `list_revisions` and `read_message`, and was slowest per call.
  - Noise: an internet drop around 21:00Z and runs sharing the same accounts.
- **Not tried:** an end-to-end run with resolver and submit, an Atira sandbox run, repeated runs.

## 2. 08dd4a6f (custom browser harness)
- **Architecture:** `login_qwen.py` loops one tool call per turn. The prompt is about 300 tokens with 7 tools; each turn sends an `aria_snapshot` of up to 5K characters, older pages are cut to 300 characters, thinking is off. A screenshot fallback was proposed.
- **Results:** the Qwen run (`out/login-qwen-20261010-213620`) never wrote a `results.json`, so there are no numbers. The thread then switched to Haiku in Claude Code learning verb click paths:
  - code-verb: 12/13 verbs replayed, 200 s, $0.31
  - code-site: 12/13, 428 s, $0.21
  - mcp-site: 13/13, 384 s, $0.34
- **Failures:** the ERP refuses broad searches without a Kataloggruppe, and mail counts drift while a run is going.
- **Not tried:** Qwen on verbs, any full run.

## 3. 7a540a56 (Qwen extraction cost)
- **Analysis only, no new runs.** It cites Qwen run `run_935ad`, an earlier full agent: calls producing 7–8.5K output tokens took 3–4 minutes each (about 35 tok/s). The five slowest took about 17.5 minutes. Some calls looked duplicated by 60 s timeout retries. It also mentions a 12-minute queue wait in one run and a 22 s average per ERP call.
- **Diagnosis:** model output was the cost, from thinking or from copying rows into `save_facts`. `llm_agent.py` didn't turn thinking off.
- **Proposed:** model points, code extracts (`read_table`), or Clef. One Clef test answered in 0.8–2.5 s, 745 tokens, about $0.0002. Clef was never wired into anything.

## 4. 9b88627c (Qwen and DeepSeek)
- **Content:** re-analyses the three-way run (same numbers as thread 1, the 21:25Z run). Also covers the cost floor (cost counts as at least $0.01) and that `goals.py` needs no account isolation, since a second session on the same account doesn't log out the first (ERP included).
- **Then Haiku only:** `paths_haiku.py`, where Haiku finds the entry point and code dumps the anchored neighbourhood.
  - Tender 1 call, ERP material 3–4 calls, ERP search 6–7, mail 2–6.
  - Spec document 0/2 (Haiku loops). Logins unreliable: mail failed 4 of 5.
  - Q&A captured only 2 of 6 pages (a depth bug). Mail dump took 300 s.
- **Qwen:** none after 21:30Z.

## 5. b119029a (DeepSeek click paths)
- **Architecture:** `htmlswarm/swarm.py`. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash only, no Qwen. It sees each tab's whole cleaned HTML and returns one action; 4 browsers with any number of tabs and a shared notes board. An address book of learned URL patterns was added later. Each site's saved pages are then extracted into the evidence schema.
- **Results** (23:10Z–00:16Z), no answer in any run:
  - 510 s, $0.12
  - 575 s, $0.34
  - 627 s, $0.39, with 3.7M input tokens
- **Failures:**
  - The resolver always stopped on missing evidence. Last run: two Kataloggruppen never searched, one stock value missing, the Rüstpools mail not found, and a quantity mismatch on position 01.05.
  - DeepSeek repeated the same blocked click 20 times and declared "done" too early.
  - The condenser initially dropped canvas text.
- **Not tried:** Qwen, a required-evidence check before a tab may stop.

## 6. 435ea8b6 (cheap click-path pipeline)
- **Architecture:** `erp_chain.py`, ERP only, no Qwen.
  - Haiku logs in and finds the first search; code replays the other 4 groups.
  - Opus (low reasoning) picks candidates; Haiku opens the first material.
  - Code follows the anchored links and fetches 9 materials × 11–15 screens with `fetch()`; code also does the text cleanup.
- **Results:** 156/156 values captured, 78 s, $0.029. Opus was $0.026 of that.
- **Notes:**
  - The Kataloggruppen were fed in from an earlier run's results, not found by the agent. That's a shortcut for the local test; it would break fair play in a package.
  - DeepSeek as cleaner lost values (output truncated, inconsistent line drops).
- **Not tried:** spec and mail chains, Evidence JSON into `resolver.py`, submit, Qwen.

## Overall verdict
1. A partial attempt exists: Qwen as a stateless pointer in `goals.py`, at about 1K tokens and 1 action per call. It was only tested on 16 sub-goals: best 13/16, 277 s, about $0.018. It never ran end to end, so it has no quality score.
2. It fell short of 100 mainly because the harness was never finished, not because of the model. Causes: finish-condition bugs, the `verbindlich` block, incomplete mail paging, unreliable logins, no research→resolver→submit wiring, and no Atira sandbox run.
3. Qwen-specific problems were slow calls (4.7 s each, versus 1.5 s for Haiku), the earlier ERP gate loop, and in older full-agent runs thinking/output-heavy 3–4 min calls and queue waits. All of these were measured before the 2026-10-11 00:07 UTC speed-up, so they may be stale.
4. Never tried: Qwen on the "model picks the entry point, code dumps/fetches the neighbourhood" pattern that worked in `erp_chain.py` (78 s for all ERP data), Qwen as the orchestrator or picker in place of Opus, and Clef for the choice calls.
5. The pieces add up to roughly the leaders' budget (logins plus a few entry points, then code dumps plus a resolver), but none of the threads put them together into one run.
